source.title: Memorization Capacity of Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
source.authors: Sadegh Mahdavi; Ren-Jie Liao; Christos Thrampoulidis

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are not stated in text and cannot be read precisely from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses synthetic experiments with gradient-based optimization to test memorization by a single-layer multi-head attention model. This bears on fitting random labels, but it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments or evaluate test error.
record.gate_note: The paper also proves an existence bound for fitting arbitrary labels, but that is not a training result. Figure 2 reports average training accuracy for uniform labels across sweeps of heads, context size, and dataset size; precise plotted values are figure-only. Appendix H states the largest dataset sizes found to be perfectly memorized for H=4 and H=8. Cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures training accuracy on iid random labels in a new setting: synthetic inputs and a single-layer attention model trained with Adam. These experiments bear on V1's fitting component; the existence theorem alone does not establish gradient-based fitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors prove an arbitrary-label capacity lower bound under linear-independence assumptions and empirically confirm effects of head count, context length, and head dimension. They distinguish existence from optimization and caution that gradient-based memorization can require tuning and many updates.
record.recipe_differences: A single-layer attention-only model is trained on synthetic data with Adam. The study examines memorization capacity and optimization behavior, rather than reproducing the original deep-network random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Memorization changes with head count, context size, and head dimension; the paper reports that optimization can be challenging and that larger head dimensions can improve optimization speed.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 proves that suitable attention weights exist to memorize arbitrary labels under specified linear-independence assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-layer attention has an arbitrary-label representational capacity lower bound of H(min(n, dh)−1)+1 examples under the stated assumptions.

record.problems: Experiments are synthetic and use an attention-only model. The authors caution that gradient descent is not guaranteed to find a memorizing solution and may require extensive steps and hyperparameter tuning. Individual Figure 2 values are not given in text. No test error or true-label comparison is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 reports average accuracies over multiple head counts, context sizes, and dataset sizes, but the supplied text does not give individual plotted values. These figure-only outcomes are summarized in R3 rather than creating rows with unassignable numerical values. Figure 3 reports softmax saturation counts and distributions, not training accuracy itself.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to true-label training, and fitting by standard deep networks rather than this attention-only model.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence as label corruption increases. Optimization caveats and head-dimension effects do not measure either comparison.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs. The synthetic inputs here are uniform random vectors.
A label-corruption sweep with training and test errors.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels.

missing.what: Random-label classification experiments with independently generated contexts and queries are omitted. Figure 4a,c reports training accuracy across head-count, context-size, and dataset-size conditions; Appendix I.1 states that head-count linearity remains while context-size linearity weakens. Exact accuracies require the figure and cannot be reconstructed here. These conditions need separate rows before assigning fitting verdicts.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V1 limits_scope label based solely on the restricted architecture and missing test-error or true-label comparisons: these are untested parts, not demonstrated failures. Figure 2's scaling trends alone do not establish which individual conditions achieve near-zero training error.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments test fitting synthetic uniform labels with an attention-only model. They do not report test error or show that it is at chance, compare true labels with random labels, or establish the claim across standard deep networks.
